title: A Summer ABoVE the Warming Arctic
description: Scientists with NASA's Arctic Boreal Vulnerability Experiment - ABoVE - are studying how the Arctic region responds to climate change. Looking at everything from thawing permafrost underground to wildfires, the researchers are working to create a comprehensive picture of the warming Arctic.  This summer, the team brought a fleet of planes to fly over Alaska and Canada and gather data to complement measurements taken from the ground. The ABoVE campaign is designed to last for ten years.
keywords: Carbon Release, Carbon Sink, Climate, Climate Indicators, Organic Matter, Permafrost, Arctic, Climate Change, Earth, Wildfires
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: The Arctic is getting greener and wetter, warming roughly twice as fast as the rest of the planet.
This summer, NASA scientists took a bird's eye view, several of them in fact, to study changes in the region.
As part of the Arctic Boreal Vulnerability Experiment, or above, scientists from NASA and partner organizations
pull out a total of 10 planes over Alaska and Canada to gather important instrument data,
measuring everything from carbon in the atmosphere to water levels in lakes and rivers and thawing per frost.
These data will be combined with measurements taken from field sites to get a comprehensive picture of environmental change in the Arctic.
On the active sensing of carbon dioxide emissions over nice days and seasons for a SENS experiment,
NASA's DC-8 plane flew big, looping spirals over Alaska and Canada to measure carbon dioxide and methane released into the atmosphere.
Scientists down on the tundra are looking for sources and sinks with carbon dioxide and methane.
NASA's partner organizations are studying emissions from thawing perma-thrust, using plexiglass boxes that sit directly on the ground,
as well as small towers that measure how carbon dioxide, methane and energy move from the land surface to the atmosphere and back.
Attacking the research from multiple vantage points helps the scientists in the air ensure that their instruments are functioning properly and test them against known measurements.
In addition, it can help the science teams pinpoint the potential causes of changes their instruments read.
For the SENS team, that may mean determining if carbon spikes they see in the air are from wildfires or organic materials decomposing underground.
With the summer over in the Arctic, the above teams finish with a second year of research in the region.
Next summer, they'll be back in the field to collect another round of data.
The campaign is designed to run for 10 years to provide a look at long-term trends caused by the warming climate.
